| `generate_referral` | implemented | `BaseCase::generate_referral` | A real click-through: it opens start_page (an empty string means the current page), builds a link to destination_page in it with a script and clicks it, so the destination receives a Referer header. With a selector, that element is clicked on the destination page too. Differs: Builds the link with DOM calls and quotes the URL, where Python pastes it into markup; waits for the destination's readyState after the click, where Python only pauses 0.15 s. An invalid page is SeleniumBaseError::Parse, checked before the browser is touched. |
| `generate_referral_chain` | implemented | `BaseCase::generate_referral_chain` | Takes a slice of pages. Builds and clicks a link to each page in turn, starting from the page the browser is on, so each page after the first sees the one before it as its Referer. Differs: Fewer than two pages is SeleniumBaseError::InvalidConfig and an invalid page is SeleniumBaseError::Parse, both before the first click (Python raises plain exceptions). |

A session that is not Firefox gets an Unsupported error. Tested against a mock WebDriver for the exact endpoint and JSON body. Checked against a real geckodriver 0.37.1 and Firefox 153 ESR in Docker (docker/firefox-check): the same bodies sent with curl installed a directory and an .xpi, the add-on's content script ran, and the uninstall stopped it; tests/install_addon_firefox.rs (ignored) runs BaseCase against that geckodriver and installs and removes an add-on. Differs: Takes a temporary flag where Python's install_addon always installs a temporary add-on, and returns the id. Sends geckodriver the path, where Python's Selenium reads the file and sends it as base64, so the file has to be on the machine geckodriver runs on. ## CDP Mode methods

Python `sb.cdp.*`; Rust holds the selector in a `Locator`.

| Upstream | Status | Rust | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `activate_cdp_mode` | not-applicable |  | Already in CDP mode: sb_cdp is the CDP engine. |
| `activate_messenger` | implemented | `Page::activate_messenger` | Loads jQuery and the Messenger library from their CDNs into the page; a page with no network cannot. |
| `add_handler` | not-applicable |  | Subscribe to protocol events with Page::events / Browser::events. |
| `append_data_to_logs` | not-applicable |  | Write files with std::fs; artifacts::ensure_latest_logs_dir gives the logs folder. |
| `assert_any_of_elements_present` | composed | `Page::wait_for_any` | `page.wait_for_any(..)` waits until one of several locators is ready and says which; it returns a timeout error where Python raises. |
| `assert_any_of_elements_visible` | composed | `Page::wait_for_any` | `page.wait_for_any(..)` waits until one of several locators is ready and says which; it returns a timeout error where Python raises. |
| `assert_downloaded_file` | implemented | `Page::assert_downloaded_file` | `page.assert_downloaded_file(name, timeout)` waits for the file in Browser::download_dir (the folder last given to set_download_dir or to a Page download method) and returns its path. A download the browser has not finished does not count. Differs: Looks in the folder the browser was told to save in, where Python always looks in ./downloaded_files (that is the default until a folder is chosen). Fails with SeleniumBaseError::WaitTimeout, where Python raises NoSuchFileException, and takes a Duration. The name must be a plain file name. |
| `assert_element` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_be_visible` | Assert with `page.locator(selector).expect().to_be_visible(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_element_absent` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_exist` | `page.locator(selector).expect().not().to_exist()`; the wait is the expect timeout. |
| `assert_element_attribute` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_have_attribute` | Assert with `page.locator(selector).expect().to_have_attribute(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_element_not_visible` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_be_hidden` | `page.locator(selector).expect().to_be_hidden()`; the wait is the expect timeout. |
| `assert_element_present` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_exist` | `page.locator(selector).expect().to_exist()`; the wait is the expect timeout. |
| `assert_element_visible` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_be_visible` | Assert with `page.locator(selector).expect().to_be_visible(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_equal` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_exact_text` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_have_text` | `page.locator(selector).expect().to_have_text(text)`, which compares the whole text. |
| `assert_false` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_in` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_not_equal` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_not_in` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_text` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_contain_text` | Assert with `page.locator(selector).expect().to_contain_text(..)` (the text of an &lt;input&gt; or &lt;textarea&gt; is its value, as in Python); add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_text_not_visible` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_contain_text` | `page.locator(selector).expect().not().to_contain_text(text)`; the wait is the expect timeout. |
| `assert_title` | composed | `PageExpect::to_have_title` | Assert with `page.expect().to_have_title(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_title_contains` | composed | `PageExpect::to_contain_title` | Assert with `page.expect().to_contain_title(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_true` | not-applicable |  | Rust has assert!, assert_eq! and friends. |
| `assert_url` | composed | `PageExpect::to_have_url` | Assert with `page.expect().to_have_url(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `assert_url_contains` | composed | `PageExpect::to_contain_url` | Assert with `page.expect().to_contain_url(..)`; add `.not()` to negate and `.timeout(d)` to set the wait. A failed expectation returns an error where Python raises AssertionError. |
| `bring_active_window_to_front` | composed | `Page::bring_to_front` | A method of the Page that sb.cdp drives: `page.bring_to_front(..)`. |
| `check_if_unchecked` | composed | `Locator::check` | Call `page.locator(selector).check(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `clear` | composed | `Locator::clear` | Call `page.locator(selector).clear(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `clear_cookies` | composed | `Cookies::clear` | `page.cookies().clear(..)`. |
| `clear_input` | composed | `Locator::clear` | Call `page.locator(selector).clear(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `click` | composed | `Locator::click` | Call `page.locator(selector).click(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `click_active_element` | implemented | `Page::click_active_element` | `page.click_active_element()` calls `click()` on `document.activeElement`. Differs: Does not pause for 0.2 seconds afterwards; wait for what the click causes with a Locator wait. |
| `click_and_hold` | composed | `Locator::click_and_hold` | `page.locator(selector).click_and_hold(Duration::from_secs(2))` scrolls the element into view, presses at its centre, holds for the given time and releases there. Mouse::down and Mouse::up act at coordinates. |
| `click_captcha` | composed | `Page::solve_captcha` | A method of the Page that sb.cdp drives: `page.solve_captcha(..)`. Differs: The same as `solve_captcha`: ours waits for the widget to stand still, presses along a human path and checks the result, pressing again only when the page can show a result and did not. |
| `click_if_visible` | implemented | `Locator::click_if_visible` | `page.locator(selector).click_if_visible()` clicks if the element is visible now (Python's default `timeout=0`: look once) and says whether it clicked; `click_if_visible_with_timeout(timeout)` waits up to `timeout` for it. The Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. Differs: Gives Ok(false) when the element is not visible in time or vanishes before the click; an invalid selector or a lost connection is still an error, where Python suppresses every error. The click always scrolls the element into view (`scroll=True`). |
| `click_link` | composed | `Locator::click` | `page.locator(SelectorBuf::partial_link_text(link_text)).click()` clicks the first link whose text contains `link_text`. The argument is link text, not a selector, so build the selector with `SelectorBuf::partial_link_text` (or `link_text` for an exact match) rather than passing the bare text. |
| `click_nth_element` | composed | `Locator::nth` | `page.locator(selector).nth(i).click()`; `nth` is zero-based, Python's number starts at 1. |
| `click_nth_visible_element` | composed | `Locator::nth` | `page.locator(selector).visible().nth(i).click()`; `nth` is zero-based, Python's number starts at 1. |
| `click_visible_elements` | composed | `Locator::visible` | `page.locator(selector).visible()` narrows the Locator to the displayed matches; click each with `nth`. |
| `click_with_offset` | implemented | `Locator::click_with_offset` | `page.locator(selector).click_with_offset(x, y, center)`; the offset is from the element's top-left corner, or from its centre when `center` is true, as in Python. Differs: Always scrolls the element into view (Python's `scroll=True`, its default). |
| `close_active_tab` | composed | `Page::close` | `page.close()` closes that Page's tab. |
| `download_file` | implemented | `Page::download_file` | `page.download_file(url, dir)` has the page fetch the address and save the response, as Python does, then waits for the browser to finish and returns the saved path. `page.download_by_click(selector, dir)` follows a download that a click starts. Differs: Takes the folder to save in (Python uses ./downloaded_files) and waits for the browser's own download events, bounded by the page timeout; a bad HTTP status, a fetch the page refuses (CORS) or a cancelled download is SeleniumBaseError::Download. The name comes from the Content-Disposition header when the server sends one, else from the address (Python: the address only). |
| `drag_and_drop` | composed | `Locator::drag_to` | Call `page.locator(selector).drag_to(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `enter_mfa_code` | composed | `BaseCase::enter_mfa_code` | BaseCase::enter_mfa_code is a WebDriver-engine method; on the CDP engine compute the code with BaseCase::get_mfa_code and type it with Locator::type_text. |
| `evaluate` | composed | `Page::evaluate` | `page.evaluate(script)`; values come back as serde_json::Value, so an element comes back as `{}`. As in Python, a `return ` that starts the last line is dropped; a `return` anywhere else is a syntax error, so wrap such a script in `(() => { ... })()`. |
| `execute_script` | composed | `Page::evaluate` | `page.evaluate(script)`, as for `evaluate`: a `return ` that starts the last line is dropped, so Selenium-style `return document.title` works; values come back as serde_json::Value. |
| `fast_keys` | composed | `Keyboard::insert_text` | Python types into the element the selector names. Focus it first: `page.locator(selector).focus().await?; page.keyboard().insert_text(text).await?` inserts the text in one step after what the field holds. fast_type's Locator::fill clears the field first. |
| `fast_type` | composed | `Locator::fill` | `page.locator(selector).fill(text)` replaces the content in one step, with input events but no per-key ones. |
| `find_all` | composed | `Locator::all_waiting` | `page.locator(selector).all_waiting()` waits up to the timeout for a first match, then gives one Locator per match; after the timeout it gives an empty list, as Python does. `all()` does not wait. |
| `find_element` | composed | `Page::locator` | `page.locator(selector)` returns a Locator, the handle every element action goes through; CSS, XPath and `tag:contains("text")` selectors work. Python also searches by text when the selector is plain text, which Rust does not guess: use `SelectorBuf::containing_text`. Python's `best_match` option is not offered. |
| `find_element_by_text` | composed | `SelectorBuf::containing_text` | `page.locator(SelectorBuf::containing_text(text, Some("button")))` finds a tag element whose text contains the text, as Python's `tag:contains("text")` does (that form also works as a selector string); with `None` for the tag it finds the innermost elements that hold the text. A `text=` prefix still means link text, as in SeleniumBase. |
| `find_elements` | composed | `Locator::all_waiting` | `page.locator(selector).all_waiting()` waits up to the timeout for a first match, then gives one Locator per match; after the timeout it gives an empty list, as Python does. `all()` does not wait. |
| `find_elements_by_text` | composed | `SelectorBuf::containing_text` | `page.locator(SelectorBuf::containing_text(text, tag)).all()` gives one Locator per element that contains the text: the innermost ones when `tag` is None, every `tag` element otherwise. |
| `find_visible_elements` | composed | `Locator::visible` | Call `page.locator(selector).visible(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `flash` | composed | `Locator::flash_with` | `page.locator(selector).flash_with(color, duration)` outlines the element for the duration in any CSS colour; `flash()` uses the defaults. Python's `pause` is a `tokio::time::sleep` afterwards. The outline is an outline, not Python's vanishing dot. |
| `focus` | composed | `Locator::focus` | Call `page.locator(selector).focus(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `get` | composed | `Page::goto` | A method of the Page that sb.cdp drives: `page.goto(..)`. |
| `get_active_element` | composed | `Page::active_element` | `page.active_element()` returns a Locator for the element that has focus, found through its selector. Python returns a dump of the element; read what you need from the Locator (`info()`, `text()`, `attribute(..)`). `page.evaluate("document.activeElement")` does not work: an element comes back as `{}`. |
| `get_active_element_css` | composed | `Page::active_element_css` | `page.active_element_css()` returns the shortest selector that finds the focused element, such as `input#email`, or `body` when nothing has focus. |
| `get_active_tab` | composed | `Browser::default_page` | Python's active tab is the one the engine drives; in Rust that is the Page you hold. `browser.default_page()` is only the first tab listed, which may be another one. |
| `get_all_cookies` | composed | `Cookies::all` | `page.cookies().all(..)`. |

Differs: Python presses at a fixed offset (25, 32) and returns without checking what happened; ours finds the widget in the page, its open shadow roots and the frames it may read, waits for it to stand still, presses within a few pixels of the left-edge checkbox along a human pointer path, and checks the result (a token in the response field, the clearance cookie, a page with no widget). It presses again, up to three times with a growing, spread-out wait, only when the page can show a result and did not, and then fails with `SeleniumBaseError::Captcha`; `solve_captcha_with(&SolveOptions)` says what showed it cleared. Python rewrites `center` and `right` in the page's classes and styles to `left` so that the widget moves to the corner; ours leaves the page alone. Neither reads a closed shadow root. |

| `wait_for_element_present` | composed | `Locator::wait_for` | Call `page.locator(selector).wait_for(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `wait_for_element_visible` | composed | `Locator::wait_for` | Call `page.locator(selector).wait_for(..)`; the Locator holds the selector, so it is not an argument of the call. |
| `wait_for_text` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_contain_text` | `page.locator(selector).expect().to_contain_text(text)` waits for the text; it does not return the element. |
| `wait_for_text_not_visible` | composed | `LocatorExpect::to_contain_text` | `page.locator(selector).expect().not().to_contain_text(text)` waits for the text to go. |

## Command-line commands

Python `seleniumbase` / `sbase`; Rust `sbrs`.

| Upstream | Status | Rust | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `behave-gui` | implemented | `sbrs behave-gui` | Terminal UI instead of Tkinter (feature `tui`): lists the .feature files with their scenarios, runs the ones you mark with `cargo test` (one run per feature, each scenario found by its snake-case title among the test names) and shows the results; without `tui` it prints a hint and exits with status 2, as `sbrs commander` does. `--new` keeps the earlier prompt that writes a new feature file. Differs: Python starts `python -m behave` with the browser, session, demo, dashboard, headless, screenshot and extra options. Here the scenarios run as the project's rstest-bdd tests (feature `bdd`), the only run option is a tag filter read from the feature file, and a scenario no test is named after is reported as undefined. |
| `behave-options` | implemented | `sbrs behave-options` | Prints how the behave options map to `sbrs test`: each `-D name[=value]` is the flag of the same name, `--dry-run` is `--co`, `--stop` is `--runner nextest`. Differs: Gherkin scenarios are rstest-bdd tests run by `cargo test`, so `-q/--no-snippets` has no meaning (steps are checked at compile time) and `--tags` is `scenarios!(.., tags = ..)` or `-m`. |
| `case-plans` | implemented | `sbrs caseplans` | Alias of caseplans upstream; terminal UI instead of Tkinter, as for `sbrs caseplans`, and `sbrs case-plans` (and `sbrs case_plans`) is an alias of it here too. |
| `caseplans` | implemented | `sbrs caseplans` | Terminal UI instead of Tkinter (feature `tui`): lists the Rust test functions under a folder, creates, edits and saves `case_plans/<test>.md` for each and writes `case_summary.md`; without `tui` it prints a hint and exits with status 2, as `sbrs commander` does. `--starter` keeps the earlier command that writes a fixed CASE_PLANS.md checklist. `-k FILTER` starts with the list narrowed to the test ids that contain FILTER, as `/` does in the app. Differs: Python lists what pytest collects (`file.py::Class::method`); here the test functions are found by reading the files, so a `#[test]` inside a string looks like a test. Plans and the summary are written with LF line ends, not CRLF. |
| `codegen` | composed | `sbrs record` | `sbrs record URL -o FILE` writes the recorded actions as a JSON or YAML list that `sbrs replay` runs. It does not write a test file; ActionRecorder::to_rust_test does that, from code. |
| `commander` | implemented | `sbrs commander` | `sbrs commander [PATH] [-k FILTER]`, also `sbrs gui`: a terminal menu (feature `tui`) that lists the tests and examples under PATH (a project folder, a folder of test files or one test file; by default `tests/` and `examples/`) and runs the one you pick with Cargo. `-k` starts with the list narrowed to the names that contain FILTER, as `/` does in the app; without `tui` it prints a hint and exits with status 2. Differs: Python's `-k` is a pytest expression and its `-m` a marker; here `-k` is a plain substring of the test's name (`sbrs test -k` has the pytest expression). |
| `convert` | implemented | `sbrs convert` | `sbrs convert FILE.py [--force]` reads a Selenium IDE or Katalon Recorder export (Selenium WebDriver code) with the Selenium reading of `import_python` and writes `FILE_SB.rs` next to it; the original is kept. An existing output is refused without `--force`. What it cannot convert stays a `TODO` and is listed on standard error; the exit status is 1 when a statement could not be read at all. Differs: Python's convert writes `FILE_SB.py`, a SeleniumBase class; this writes a Rust test (`run_browser_test`) named after the file. |
| `decrypt` | implemented | `sbrs decrypt` | Differs: Reads tokens made by `sbrs encrypt` only; see `encrypt`. |
| `download` | implemented | `sbrs download` | Differs: Downloads Selenium Server 4 (default 4.51.0, whose SHA-256 is pinned in the source and checked; another --version is saved with its SHA-256 and `not verified`) into downloaded_drivers/, not Python's Selenium 3.141.59, because Selenium Grid 3 is gone. `sbrs grid-hub` and `sbrs grid-node` use the newest jar there when neither --jar nor SB_SELENIUM_SERVER_JAR names one. (`sbrs download-file` downloads a file from a URL, which is another command.) |
| `encrypt` | implemented | `sbrs encrypt` | Differs: AES-256-GCM under a PBKDF2 key from SB_ENCRYPTION_KEY (asked once, without echo, when it is not set and standard input is a terminal), not Python's fixed-key obfuscation; tokens are not interchangeable. |
| `extract-objects` | not-applicable |  | Edits the structure of Python test files. |
| `get` | implemented | `sbrs get` | An alias of `sbrs install`, as in Python: `sbrs get chromedriver\|geckodriver\|edgedriver [VERSION]` (also `firefoxdriver` and `msedgedriver`). chromedriver and edgedriver default to the driver for the installed Chrome and Edge, geckodriver to the newest GitHub release; VERSION is `latest`, a major version or a full build (a geckodriver version such as 0.36.0). Each driver goes to downloaded_drivers/&lt;driver&gt;-&lt;version&gt;/. Differs: No `--path`: the driver stays in downloaded_drivers/ and is not copied to a folder on the PATH. Chrome for Testing and chrome-headless-shell are not fetched by name here; they are fetched when a session chooses one of them as the browser. |
| `grid-hub` | implemented | `sbrs grid-hub` | start, stop, restart and status; needs a Selenium Server jar you supply and Java, and downloads nothing. Python's options are `-v/--verbose` and `--timeout SECONDS` (not imposed when left out), and `sbrs grid_hub` is accepted. |
| `grid-node` | implemented | `sbrs grid-node` | start, stop, restart and status; registers with the hub named by --hub. `-v/--verbose`, `--timeout SECONDS` and the name `sbrs grid_node` are Python's. |
| `gui` | implemented | `sbrs commander` | An alias of `commander`, as in Python: `sbrs gui [PATH] [-k FILTER]`; a terminal app instead of a window. |
| `gui-behave` | implemented | `sbrs behave-gui` | Alias of behave-gui upstream; terminal UI instead of Tkinter, as for `sbrs behave-gui`, and `sbrs gui-behave` is an alias of it here too. |
| `help` | composed | `usage` | Provided by the argument parser. |
| `inject-objects` | not-applicable |  | Edits the structure of Python test files. |
| `install` | implemented | `sbrs install` | `sbrs install chromedriver\|geckodriver\|edgedriver [VERSION]`; with no argument it fetches the chromedriver that matches the installed Chrome (or the stable one). The same command as `sbrs get`. Differs: No `--path`: the driver stays in downloaded_drivers/ and is not copied to a folder on the PATH. |
| `methods` | implemented | `sbrs methods` | Prints the 43 common test methods in Rust spelling (`sb.open(url)`, `sb.type_text(selector, text)`, ...) with what each does; a test checks every one against the `basecase` rows of this file. Differs: Python's list is of `self.` calls in a TestCase; this one is of the async `BaseCase` methods, so the Rust name of a renamed method is shown (`type` is `type_text`). The whole API is `cargo doc` and docs/parity.md. |
| `mkchart` | implemented | `sbrs mkchart` | `sbrs mkchart FILE [--en\|--zh\|--nl\|--fr\|--it\|--ja\|--ko\|--pt\|--ru\|--es] [--force]` writes a Rust test (the rstest `sb` fixture) that builds a pie chart with `create_pie_chart` and `add_data_point` (six points), takes it with `extract_chart` and shows it on a slide of a `sky`/`slide` presentation, with Python's labels in the chosen language. Differs: Python writes a SeleniumBase class and prints the file; this writes a Rust test and says `Created FILE`. The method names stay English in every language. Python's French and Russian lists of chart kinds lack the commas between the names; the generated comment has them. |
| `mkdir` | implemented | `sbrs mkdir` |  |
| `mkfile` | implemented | `sbrs mkfile` |  |
| `mkpres` | implemented | `sbrs mkpres` | `sbrs mkpres FILE [--en\|--zh\|--nl\|--fr\|--it\|--ja\|--ko\|--pt\|--ru\|--es] [--force]` writes a Rust test (the rstest `sb` fixture) that builds a three-slide deck with `create_presentation` (theme `serif`, transition `slide`), `add_slide` and `begin_presentation`, with Python's slide text in the chosen language. Differs: Python writes a SeleniumBase class and prints the file; this writes a Rust test and says `Created FILE`. The method names stay English in every language, and the images are the `.image(...)` of a slide, not an `<img>` tag in its text. |
| `mkrec` | composed | `sbrs record` | Python's mkrec creates a new test file with the Recorder. `sbrs record URL -o FILE` records in a browser and writes a JSON or YAML action list that `sbrs replay` runs, not a test file; `sbrs mkrec` only writes a starter recording file and opens no browser. |
| `obfuscate` | composed | `sbrs encrypt` | Alias of encrypt upstream, as here: `sbrs obfuscate` is accepted. It encrypts a string, not a source file. Tokens are AES-256-GCM under SB_ENCRYPTION_KEY, read from the environment or asked once without echo on a terminal, and do not interchange with Python's. With no argument on a terminal it prompts in a loop as Python does (text and verification without echo; Ctrl-C prints Exiting... and exits 0). |
| `objectify` | not-applicable |  | Python's objectify rewrites the selectors of a Python test file into page-object variables, like extract-objects and inject-objects, and there is no Python source to rewrite here. `sbrs objectify` only writes a starter page_object.rs. |
| `options` | implemented | `sbrs options` | Lists the browser options: each flag, its `SB_*` variable and its settings-file key (`--markdown` for the documentation, `--all` to add the options of `sbrs test`). Differs: Python lists pytest's options; the options here are the rows of one table that is also the global `sbrs` flags, the `SB_*` variables and the settings file. |
| `print` | implemented | `sbrs print` | `sbrs print FILE [-n\|--line-numbers]` shows the file as it is; `-n` puts the line number in front of every line, right-aligned to the width of the last one. Differs: Python highlights the syntax with rich, wraps long Python lines and replaces tabs by four spaces; this prints the text unchanged (bytes that are not UTF-8 show as U+FFFD). |
| `proxy` | implemented | `sbrs proxy` | Differs: A minimal forward proxy for HTTP and CONNECT on 127.0.0.1:8899 (--hostname, --port), with no authentication and no TLS interception; it warns when it listens on a non-loopback address. proxy.py's other options are not offered. |
| `record` | implemented | `sbrs record` |  |
| `recorder` | implemented | `sbrs recorder` | Python's Recorder Desktop App as a terminal app (build with the `tui` feature; without it the command prints a hint and exits with status 2). A form for the file name, the start URL, Overwrite, the browser (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Opera, Brave, Comet), Stealth Mode / UC, the output format (test, `--rec-sb-mgr` script, `--rec-sb-cdp`, Gherkin) and `--ee`; Record runs `sbrs mkrec FILE --url=URL --headed ...` with the terminal handed to it, Run starts `cargo test --test NAME` (or `cargo run --example`) and Replay runs `sbrs replay recordings/NAME_rec.json`, with a Demo Mode box for both. `--url`, `--browser`, `--uc`/`--cdp`, `--ee`, `--rec-behave`, `--rec-sb-mgr` and `--rec-sb-cdp` fill the form in at the start, as Python reads `--uc`, `--behave` and `--ee`. Differs: Python opens a Tkinter window that stays open while the recording runs in another process, and its Playback buttons run the Python file. Here Record suspends the terminal UI until `mkrec` ends (the person types `c` and Enter in that terminal, or presses SHIFT+ESC with `--ee`), because `mkrec` reads the terminal; Run needs the test in `tests/` or `examples/` (cargo runs a test by its file name) and Replay needs no compile. The file is a `.rs` name, and it is not asked before overwriting: Overwrite is a box, ticked to begin with, as in Python. |
| `revert-objects` | not-applicable |  | Edits the structure of Python test files. |
| `translate` | implemented | `sbrs translate` | sbrs translate FILE --LANG [-p\|--print] [-o\|--overwrite] [-c\|--copy] [-n\|--line-numbers] rewrites the action of every step of a JSON scenario with the translation dictionary; Scenario::from_json reads actions in any of the ten languages. LANG is Python's language flag (--zh, --chinese or --Chinese, ...) and is required; the action is print by default, -p may go with -o or -c, and -c writes FILE_LANG.json. Differs: Python translates the method calls of a Python test file. A Rust test is compiled code with English method names, so the file translated here is the JSON scenario. |
| `unobfuscate` | composed | `sbrs decrypt` | Alias of decrypt upstream, as here: `sbrs unobfuscate` is accepted. Tokens are AES-256-GCM under SB_ENCRYPTION_KEY, read from the environment or asked once without echo on a terminal, and do not interchange with Python's. With no argument on a terminal it asks for a token on the screen in a loop as Python does (Ctrl-C prints Exiting... and exits 0). |
| `version` | implemented | `sbrs version` | Prints the same line as `sbrs --version`. |

| `--account` | not-applicable |  | Hands a free-text account string to pytest tests as sb.account; a Rust test reads its own values from std::env or a fixture file. |
| `--ad-block` | composed | `BrowserConfig::ad_block` | `sbrs --ad-block` sets BrowserConfig::ad_block. Refuses the requests of the ad and tracker hosts of an AdBlockList (the built-in list, or the one set with BrowserConfig::with_ad_block_list) with Network.setBlockedURLs, which a WebDriver session sends through chromedriver's DevTools channel when it connects and for each window it switches to. Works in a Chromium WebDriver session (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Comet, Opera, Chrome for Testing, chrome-headless-shell); Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer have no DevTools channel through WebDriver and block nothing. The pure CDP engine blocks hosts with LaunchOptionsBuilder::ad_block. Python hides the ad elements of a loaded page, which BaseCase::ad_block does when called. A URL that names a port is not matched, and a frame of another site is not stopped from loading and its own requests are not blocked (a frame of the page's own site is). Checked in a real Chrome 155 with chromedriver 155 on macOS (tests/ad_block_chrome.rs). |

Also `sbrs --rcs` (aliases `--reuse-class-session`, `--reuse_class_session`), `Settings::reuse_class_session` and SB_REUSE_CLASS_SESSION; like upstream it turns --reuse-session on. Rust has no test classes, so the module that holds the test plays the part: it is read from the name libtest gives the test's thread (`login::tests::valid` is in `login::tests`; the tests at the root of an integration test file share the root module). BrowserConfig::with_reuse_class_session(name) shares a browser among the tests that pass the same name instead. Tests of different classes never share a browser; the rest is as for --reuse-session. Differs: Python quits the class's browser when the next class starts (setUpClass and tearDownClass); here it stays open until the idle timeout, so the browsers of several modules can be open at once. A BaseCase made outside a libtest thread (a custom harness, a spawned task on a Tokio worker) counts as the root module. |

| `--rec-behave` | implemented | `ActionRecorder::to_gherkin` | Writes a feature for the common browser steps; save_recording_as_feature saves it. |

With it on, BaseCase::export_recording_as_rust (and so save_recording_to_logs, `sbrs run-scenario` and the `save` command of record_live_session) returns ActionRecorder::to_cdp_script: a #[tokio::main] program of sb_cdp Page and Locator calls, every selector and value a Rust string literal. to_cdp_test and save_recording_as_cdp_test write a test; BaseCase::export_recording_as_cdp_rust asks for it whatever the setting is. 51 recorded actions have a pure CDP call, and the program written for all of them is compiled against the real sb_cdp API by tests/recorder_cdp_compiles.rs; any other action becomes a `// skipped:` comment that quotes its BaseCase call. Differs: Python writes the recording file when the test ends; here it is written when export_recording_as_rust, save_recording_to_logs or a CLI command asks. The test itself still runs on WebDriver, and the generated program launches a pure CDP Browser. Waits use the pure CDP engine's own timeout, not ten seconds, and actions with no pure CDP call (frame, window and alert switching, JavaScript clicks, set_window_size) are comments, where Python comments out the actions CDPMethods lacks. |

Also `sbrs --reuse-class-session` and SB_REUSE_CLASS_SESSION. See --rcs. Differs: See --rcs: the module plays the part of the class, and a class's browser closes after the idle timeout, not when the next class starts. |
| `--reuse-session` | implemented | `BrowserConfig::with_reuse_session` | Also `sbrs --reuse-session` (aliases `--reuse_session`, `--rs`), `Settings::reuse_session` and SB_REUSE_SESSION. BaseCase::new (BrowserSession::connect) leases an idle browser started with the same configuration (all of it but the start page) from a process-wide registry that keeps each browser's WebDriver server address, session id, capabilities and the chromedriver this crate started; it attaches with a new client made in the test's own Tokio runtime, then cleans the browser: an open dialog dismissed, every window but the first closed, every cookie deleted only with --crumbs (Network.clearBrowserCookies on Chromium, WebDriver's delete-all elsewhere), the open page's local and session storage cleared, about:blank, and the start page if there is one. BaseCase::quit, run_browser_test and dropping the case give it back open. One test holds a browser at a time; one that starts while every matching browser is held gets its own, kept for reuse too. A browser that no longer answers is closed and replaced; get_new_driver browsers are never shared. Idle browsers are closed with their chromedriver after reuse::idle_timeout (5 s; reuse::set_idle_timeout, SB_REUSE_IDLE_SECS), by seleniumbase_rs::shutdown_reused_sessions() and by common::shutdown::drain_cleanups (which sbrs calls). Mock WebDriver tests in browser::reuse check that the second case sends no new-session request (from another Tokio runtime) and which cleaning commands it sends; tests/reuse_session_chrome.rs (ignored) checks in Chrome 155 that two #[tokio::test] in one binary share one Chrome (the same session id), that the first test's cookie and local storage are gone in the second, and that the reaper closes the browser and stops chromedriver after the idle timeout. Differs: Cookies are kept unless --crumbs is given, as in Python; unlike Python, the page is always set to about:blank and the page's local and session storage cleared, and the other windows closed, because Rust tests run in any order and side by side. Python quits the shared browser when pytest ends; a Rust test binary has no end-of-run hook, so the idle timeout does it, and a binary that exits sooner after its last test leaves that browser and its chromedriver running unless shutdown_reused_sessions() is called. Under cargo-nextest each test is a process of its own and nothing is shared. |

Differs: See --rcs: the module plays the part of the class, and a class's browser closes after the idle timeout, not when the next class starts. |

Differs: See --reuse-session: cookies are kept unless --crumbs is given, the page and its storage are always reset, and the browser closes after an idle timeout, since a test binary has no end-of-run hook. |

## `SB()` arguments

Keyword arguments of `SB()`.

| Upstream | Status | Rust | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `account` | not-applicable |  | Hands a free-text account string to SB() tests as sb.account; a Rust test reads its own values from std::env or a fixture file. |
| `ad_block` | composed | `BrowserConfig::ad_block` | Set BrowserConfig::ad_block (BrowserConfig::with_ad_block). Refuses the requests of the ad and tracker hosts of an AdBlockList (the built-in list, or the one set with BrowserConfig::with_ad_block_list) with Network.setBlockedURLs, which a WebDriver session sends through chromedriver's DevTools channel when it connects and for each window it switches to. Works in a Chromium WebDriver session (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Comet, Opera, Chrome for Testing, chrome-headless-shell); Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer have no DevTools channel through WebDriver and block nothing. The pure CDP engine blocks hosts with LaunchOptionsBuilder::ad_block. Python hides the ad elements of a loaded page, which BaseCase::ad_block does when called. A URL that names a port is not matched, and a frame of another site is not stopped from loading and its own requests are not blocked (a frame of the page's own site is). Checked in a real Chrome 155 with chromedriver 155 on macOS (tests/ad_block_chrome.rs). |
| `ad_block_on` | composed | `BrowserConfig::ad_block` | Set BrowserConfig::ad_block (BrowserConfig::with_ad_block). Refuses the requests of the ad and tracker hosts of an AdBlockList (the built-in list, or the one set with BrowserConfig::with_ad_block_list) with Network.setBlockedURLs, which a WebDriver session sends through chromedriver's DevTools channel when it connects and for each window it switches to. Works in a Chromium WebDriver session (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Comet, Opera, Chrome for Testing, chrome-headless-shell); Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer have no DevTools channel through WebDriver and block nothing. The pure CDP engine blocks hosts with LaunchOptionsBuilder::ad_block. Python hides the ad elements of a loaded page, which BaseCase::ad_block does when called. A URL that names a port is not matched, and a frame of another site is not stopped from loading and its own requests are not blocked (a frame of the page's own site is). Checked in a real Chrome 155 with chromedriver 155 on macOS (tests/ad_block_chrome.rs). |

## `Driver()` arguments

Keyword arguments of `Driver()`.

| Upstream | Status | Rust | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ad_block` | composed | `BrowserConfig::ad_block` | Set BrowserConfig::ad_block (BrowserConfig::with_ad_block). Refuses the requests of the ad and tracker hosts of an AdBlockList (the built-in list, or the one set with BrowserConfig::with_ad_block_list) with Network.setBlockedURLs, which a WebDriver session sends through chromedriver's DevTools channel when it connects and for each window it switches to. Works in a Chromium WebDriver session (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Comet, Opera, Chrome for Testing, chrome-headless-shell); Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer have no DevTools channel through WebDriver and block nothing. The pure CDP engine blocks hosts with LaunchOptionsBuilder::ad_block. Python hides the ad elements of a loaded page, which BaseCase::ad_block does when called. A URL that names a port is not matched, and a frame of another site is not stopped from loading and its own requests are not blocked (a frame of the page's own site is). Checked in a real Chrome 155 with chromedriver 155 on macOS (tests/ad_block_chrome.rs). |
| `ad_block_on` | composed | `BrowserConfig::ad_block` | Set BrowserConfig::ad_block (BrowserConfig::with_ad_block). Refuses the requests of the ad and tracker hosts of an AdBlockList (the built-in list, or the one set with BrowserConfig::with_ad_block_list) with Network.setBlockedURLs, which a WebDriver session sends through chromedriver's DevTools channel when it connects and for each window it switches to. Works in a Chromium WebDriver session (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, Comet, Opera, Chrome for Testing, chrome-headless-shell); Firefox, Safari and Internet Explorer have no DevTools channel through WebDriver and block nothing. A URL that names a port is not matched, and a frame of another site is not stopped from loading and its own requests are not blocked (a frame of the page's own site is). Checked in a real Chrome 155 with chromedriver 155 on macOS (tests/ad_block_chrome.rs). |
